deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of Gauss's mathematical diary (Tagebuch), Oct 1796 to Jan 1797. Most entries are terse announcements, roughly entries 40-50 in the usual numbering (the exact numbers are from memory and approximate). Only the last block contains an actual computation.

(1) 9 Oct 1796, Sunday (the sun symbol marks Sunday; 9 Oct 1796 was a Sunday). Let p be prime and z a primitive p-th root of unity. Then no relation a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + ... + a_{p-1} z^{p-1} = 0 holds with integers a_i not all zero. Equivalently, z,...,z^{p-1} are linearly independent over Q, i.e. the cyclotomic polynomial Phi_p = x^{p-1}+...+1 is irreducible over Q. This is the key lemma behind Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 341ff and the theory of periods.

(2) 16 Oct. Results on 'multipliers of equations' chosen so that certain terms are eliminated. This continues the Tschirnhaus-type transformation and elimination ideas on the previous page (Sept 14-17). No details are given.

(3) 18 Oct. 'Law discovered; when it is also proved, we shall have brought the system to perfection.' The content is not stated. In context it probably concerns cyclotomic periods or cubic residues (cf. the Oct 1 entry on the previous page).

(4) 21 Oct. 'Vicimus GEGAN' ('we have conquered GEGAN'), marked with an asterisk. The meaning is famously unknown.

(5) 25 Nov, Göttingen. 'An elegant interpolation formula.' Not specified.

(6) 26 Nov. Gauss began expanding eta(w) = 1 - 2^-w + 3^-w - ... as a power series in w. In modern terms this is the Taylor expansion of the Dirichlet eta function eta(s) = (1-2^{1-s}) zeta(s) about s = 0. Its first terms are eta(0) = 1/2 and eta'(0) = (1/2) log(pi/2) (my computation, not on the page).

(7) Dec. Trigonometric formulas expressed by series.

(8) 23 Dec. 'Most general differentiations.' Possibly differentiation of arbitrary order; this is uncertain.

(9) 26 Dec. Gauss undertook to find the area under the parabolic curve (polynomial) passing through any number of given points. This is quadrature by integrating the interpolating polynomial (Newton-Cotes), the precursor of his 1814 'Methodus nova integralium valores per approximationem inveniendi'.

(10) 27 Dec. 'I discovered a genuine proof of Lagrange's theorem.' Given the series-reversion work on the previous page, this is most likely the Lagrange inversion (series reversion) theorem.

(11) 7 Jan 1797. Reduction of trigonometric root integrals to integrals in y with sqrt(1-y^4), i.e. lemniscatic type.
(a) Put y^2 = sin x. Then dx = 2y dy/sqrt(1-y^4) and sqrt(sin x) = y, so int sqrt(sin x) dx = 2 int y^2 dy/sqrt(1-y^4).
(c) With the same substitution, sqrt(1/sin x) = 1/y, so int dx/sqrt(sin x) = 2 int dy/sqrt(1-y^4). This is exactly the lemniscatic integral studied on the next page (Jan 8).
(b) Put y^2 = cos x. Then dx = -2y dy/sqrt(1-y^4) and sqrt(tan x) = (1-y^4)^{1/4}/y, so int sqrt(tan x) dx = -2 int dy/(1-y^4)^{1/4}. The bracket note 'yy = sin x / cos x' means y^2 = sin x for (a) and (c), and y^2 = cos x for (b). It does not mean y^2 = tan x.
errors: Formula (b) as written, int sqrt(tan x) dx = 2 int dy/(1-y^4)^(1/4), omits a minus sign: with y^2 = cos x the integrand is -2 dy/(1-y^4)^(1/4). This is harmless if limits are reversed (x from 0 corresponds to y from 1), but it is a sign slip as stated.

If the bracket were read as y^2 = tan x (as the machine transcription suggests), formula (b) would be false: that substitution gives the elementary 2 int y^2 dy/(1+y^4). The correct reading is y^2 = sin x or cos x.
The remaining entries are announcements without derivations, so there is nothing further to check.

results.what: Integer linear combinations of the primitive p-th roots of unity z,...,z^(p-1) cannot vanish (linear independence over Q; irreducibility of Phi_p)
results.modern_name: Irreducibility of the p-th cyclotomic polynomial / linear independence of primitive roots of unity

results.what: Elimination of terms of equations by multipliers (Tschirnhaus-type transformations)

results.usually_credited_to: Newton, Lagrange; Gauss's own interpolation theory c. 1805

results.what: Expansion of 1 - 2^-w + 3^-w - ... in powers of w
results.modern_name: Taylor expansion of the Dirichlet eta function at s=0 (related to Stieltjes constants)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (eta(0)=1/2, functional equation, 1749); Stieltjes (1885) for constants

results.what: Trigonometric formulas by series; most general differentiations
results.modern_name: Trigonometric series; possibly fractional or general-order differentiation

results.what: Quadrature of the polynomial through arbitrarily many given points
Reduction of int sqrt(sin x), int sqrt(tan x), int 1/sqrt(sin x) to integrals in sqrt(1-y^4) and (1-y^4)^(1/4)
results.modern_name: Reduction to lemniscatic (elliptic) integrals by substitution

deep.surprise_reason: This is the famous, published and extensively commented diary of Gauss (entries c. 40-50). The cyclotomic irreducibility lemma is in the Disquisitiones. The integral substitutions are routine and are the well-known prelude to his lemniscate work of 8 Jan 1797. Nothing here is unknown to historians.

checkable.asserts: With y^2=sin x, 2*y^2*dy/sqrt(1-y^4) = sqrt(sin x) dx (value ~0)
With y^2=cos x, -2*dy/(1-y^4)^(1/4) = sqrt(tan x) dx (value ~0), so Gauss's formula holds up to sign
eta(0)=1/2 and eta'(0)=log(pi/2)/2: the first terms of the power series Gauss began on Nov 26
Phi_p is irreducible over Q for primes p (each list has one factor), equivalent to the Oct 9 claim

checkable.sympy: t,a,b,c=symbols('t a b c'); P=interpolate([(0,a),(1,b),(2,c)],t); simplify(integrate(P,(t,0,2)) - Rational(1,3)*(a+4*b+c))
checkable.asserts: Quadrature of the parabola through given points gives Newton-Cotes rules (Simpson's rule example)

transcription_corrections: The bracketed note should read 'yy = sin x' or 'cos x' (sin written above cos, meaning y^2 = sin x for the 1st and 3rd integrals and y^2 = cos x for the 2nd). It should not be read as \frac{\sin}{\cos}x = tan x.
In the second integral there is a struck-out mark beneath the factor 2; the denominator is the fourth root of (1-y^4), as transcribed.
The ☉ before Oct 9 and Oct 16 is the astronomical symbol for Sunday (both dates were Sundays in 1796), not a mathematical sign.
'expressae' appears in the manuscript as 'expresse'; 'per Dec.' (through December) stands on its own line above 'Dec. 23'.
'quotcunque' appears in the manuscript as 'quotcunque/quolcunque', i.e. quotcunque (any number of points).
